\alpha + \beta + \gamma =$2$

\alpha\beta ( \alpha + \beta ) + \beta\gamma ( \beta + \gamma ) + \gamma\alpha ( \gamma + \alpha )

\alpha\beta ($2 - $\gamma ) + \beta\gamma ($2 - $\alpha ) + \gamma\alpha ($2 - $\beta )

$= 2\mathop{∑}_{}$\alpha\beta -$3$\alpha\beta\gamma

$= 2 ( 3 ) - 3 $\times$4$

$= - 6$

questions.q: The remainder obtained by dividing the polynomial x<sup>100</sup> by the polynomial x<sup>2</sup> - 3x + 2 is equal to
questions.solution:
Concept Involved
Remainder Theorem& If a polynomial P(x) is divided by \left(\text{x} - α\right)$,~then the remainder obtained is equal to $\text{p} \left(α\right)$.

Dividend x100
Divisor x2 - 3x + 2 = (x - 1) (x - 2)

Let P(x) = x100

= (x - 1) (x - 2) Q(x) + R(x) ~ ~ ~ \text{ and } ...(i)

Since, the divisor is a quadratic, hence the degree of remainder should be less than 2 (i.e., $≤$~1).
Let us assume that the remainder obtained is R(x) = ax + b, then to find R(x), we have to basically find the values of a and b.
On substituting x = 1 in Eq. (i) we get

P(1) = 1100 = (1 - 1) (x - 2) Q (x) + R(1)

→ ~R(1) = 1

→ ~a + b = 1 \text{ and } \text{ and } \text{ and } \text{ and } \text{ and } \text{ and } \text{ and } \text{ and } \text{ and } ...(ii)

On substituting x = 2 in Eq. (i) we get

P(2) = 2100 = (2 - 1) (2 - 2) Q (x) + R(2)

→ \text{ and } R(2) = 2100

→ \text{ and } 2a + b = 2100 ...(iii)

On solving Eqs. (ii) and (iii), we get

a = 2200 - 1

and b = 2 - 2100

Hence, the remainder obtained is

R(x) = ax + b = (2100 - 1) x + (2 - 2100)

→ \text{ and } R(x) = (2100 - 1) x - 2(299 - 1)

Alternatively

When x100 is divided by x - 1, then the remainder obtained is 1100 .

→ \dfrac{x^{1 0 0}}{\text{x} - 1} = {q}_{1} \left(\text{x}\right) + \dfrac{1}{\text{x} - 1} ...(i)

Similarly, when x100 is divided by x - 2, the remainder obtained is 2100.

→ \dfrac{x^{1 0 0}}{\text{x} - 2} = {q}_{2} \left(\text{x}\right) + \dfrac{{2}^{1 0 0}}{\text{x} - 2}~ ~ ~ \text{ and } \text{ and } \text{ and } \text{ and } \text{ and } \text{ and } ...(ii)

On subtracting Eq. (ii) from Eq. (i), we get

\dfrac{x^{1 0 0}}{\text{x} - 1} - \dfrac{x^{1 0 0}}{\text{x} - 2} = \left[{q}_{1} \left(\text{x}\right) - {q}_{2} \left(\text{x}\right)\right] + \$left(\dfrac{1}{\text{x} - 1} - \dfrac{{2}^{1 0 0}}{\text{x} - 2}\right)

→ \dfrac{- x^{1 0 0}}{\left(\text{x} - 1\right) \left(\text{x} - 2\right)} = {q}_{1} \left(\text{x}\right) - {q}_{2} \left(\text{x}\right) + \dfrac{1}{\text{x} - 1} - \dfrac{{2}^{1 0 0}}{\text{x} - 2}

→ \dfrac{- x^{1 0 0}}{\left(\text{x} - 1\right) \left(\text{x} - 2\right)} = {q}_{2} \left(\text{x}\right) - {q}_{1} \left(\text{x}\right) + \dfrac{{2}^{1 0 0} \left(\text{x} - 1\right) - \left(\text{x} - 2\right)}{\left(\text{x} - 1\right) \left(\text{x} - 2\right)}

$∴$Remainder = 2100(x - 1) - (x - 2)
= (2100 - 1) x - 2(299 - 1)$

questions.q: The minimum value of $(x-\alpha)(x-\beta)$ is
questions.solution:
Let $y=(x-\alpha)(x-\beta)\begin{aligned} y & =x^2-(\alpha+\beta) x+\alpha \beta \\ y^{\prime} & =2 x-(\alpha+\beta)\end{aligned}$
For maximum or minimum, put $y^{\prime}=0\begin{array}{rrrl}\Rightarrow & 2 x-(\alpha+\beta) & =0 \\ \Rightarrow & x & =\frac{\alpha+\beta}{2} \\ \Rightarrow & y^{\prime \prime} & =2=+ \text { ve }\end{array}
The minimum value at $x=$\frac{\alpha+\beta}{2} is
\begin{aligned}$y & =  \left(\frac{\alpha+\beta}{2}-\alpha\right)\left(\frac{\alpha+\beta}{2}-\beta\right)$\\ & =$\frac{1}{4}(\beta-\alpha)(\alpha-\beta)=-\frac{1}{4}(\alpha-\beta)^2\end{aligned}$

questions.q: If $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are the real roots of the equation $\sqrt{\frac{5 x}{x-2}}+\sqrt{\frac{x-2}{5 x}}=\frac{29}{10}$ and $\alpha>\beta$, then $\sqrt{\alpha^2-11^4 \beta^2}=$
questions.solution: We have, $\sqrt{\frac{5 x}{x-2}}+\sqrt{\frac{x-2}{5 x}}=\frac{29}{10}$ Let $\quad \sqrt{\frac{5 x}{x-2}}=y$ Then, $y+\frac{1}{y}=\frac{29}{10} \Rightarrow \frac{y^2+1}{y}=\frac{29}{10}\Rightarrow \quad 10 y^2+10=29 y\Rightarrow \quad 10 y^2-29 y+10=0\Rightarrow \quad 10 y^2-25 y-4 y+10=0\Rightarrow \quad 5 y(2 y-5)-2(2 y-5)=0\Rightarrow \quad(5 y-2)(2 y-5)=0\Rightarrow \quad y=\frac{2}{5}, \frac{5}{2}$ Now, if $y=\frac{2}{5} \Rightarrow \sqrt{\frac{5 x}{x-2}}=\frac{2}{5}\Rightarrow \quad \frac{5 x}{x-2}=\frac{4}{25}\Rightarrow \quad 125 x=4 x-8\Rightarrow \quad 121 x=-8\Rightarrow \quad x=-8 / 121$ And if $y=\frac{5}{2} \Rightarrow \sqrt{\frac{5 x}{x-2}}=\frac{5}{2}\Rightarrow \quad \frac{5 x}{x-2}=\frac{25}{4}\Rightarrow \quad \frac{x}{x-2}=\frac{5}{4} \Rightarrow 5 x-10=4 x\Rightarrow \quad x=10\therefore$ Let $\alpha=10$ and $\beta=\frac{-8}{121}(\because \alpha>\beta)\therefore \quad \sqrt{\alpha^2-11^4 \beta^2}=\sqrt{(10)^2-11^4\left(\frac{-8}{121}\right)^2}=\sqrt{100-64}=\sqrt{36}=6$

questions.q: Let $D = a^{2} + b^{2} + c^{2},$ where $a, b$ being consecutive integers and $c = ab,$ then $\sqrt{D}$ is
questions.solution:
We have,

$D = a^{2} + b^{2} + c^{2}$

Since,~$a$~and~$b$~are consecutive integers therefore,~$b = a + 1$~and~$c = ab = a \left(a + 1\right)$. Then

$D = a^{2} + b^{2} + c^{2}$

$= a^{2} + \left(a + 1\right)2 + a^{2}\left(a + 1\right)2$

$= a^{2}\left\{1 + \left(a + 1\right)2\right\} + \left(a + 1\right)2$

$= a^{2}\left(a^{2} + 2a + 2\right) + \left(a^{2} + 2a + 1\right)$

$= a^{4} + 2a^{3} + 3a^{2} + 2a + 1$

$= \left(a^{2} + a + 1\right)2$

$∴ \sqrt{D} =$=a\left(a + 1\right) + 1 =$ an odd integer.

$

questions.solution:
We have,
$\begin{aligned} \frac{x-4}{x^2-5 x-2 k} & =\frac{2}{x-2}-\frac{1}{x+k} \\ \Rightarrow \quad \frac{x-4}{x^2-5 x-2 k} & =\frac{2(x+k)-(x-2)}{(x-2)(x+k)} \\ & =\frac{x+2 k+2}{(x-2)(x+k)}\end{aligned}$
On equating, we get
$\begin{aligned}-4 & =2 k+2 \\ 2 k & =-6 \Rightarrow k=-3\end{aligned}$

questions.q: If $\alpha, \beta, \gamma$ are the roots of the equation $x^3+a x^2+b x+c=0$, then $\alpha^{-1}+\beta^{-1}+\gamma^{-1}$ is equal to
questions.solution:
Let $\alpha, \beta, \gamma$ are roots of equation $\begin{aligned}$& x³+a x²+b x+c=0 \\
& $\alpha+\beta+\gamma=-$a \\
& \therefore \quad $\alpha \beta+\beta \gamma+\gamma \alpha=$b \\
& $\text { Now, } \alpha^{-1}+\beta^{-1}+\gamma^{-1}=\frac{1}{\alpha}+\frac{1}{\beta}+\frac{1}{\gamma}$\\
&=$\frac{\alpha \beta+\beta \gamma+\gamma \alpha}{\alpha \beta \gamma}=\frac{b}{-c}=-\frac{b}{c}
\end{aligned}$

questions.q: If $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are roots of the equation $x^{2} + 5\left|x\right| - 6 = 0$ then the value of \left|\tan^{- 1} ⁡ \alpha - \tan^{- 1} ⁡ \beta\right|$ is$
questions.solution:
$x^{2} + 5\left|x\right| - 6 = 0$
${\left|x\right|}^{2} + 5\left|x\right| - 6 = 0$
${\left|x\right|}^{2} + 6\left|x\right| - \left|x\right| - 6 = 0$
\left|x\right|\left(\left|x\right| + 6\right) - 1\left(\left|x\right| + 6\right) = 0$
\left(\left|x\right| - 1\right)\left(\left|x\right| + 6\right) = 0$
\left|x\right| = 1, \left|x\right| \ne - 6$ (Since modulus can not be giving negative values)
$∴ \left|x\right| = 1$
$∴ x = \pm 1$
$\alpha = 1, \beta = - 1$
$∴ \left|\tan^{- 1} ⁡ \alpha - \tan^{- 1} ⁡ \beta\right| = \left|\tan^{- 1} ⁡ 1 - \tan^{- 1} ⁡ \left(- 1\right)\right|$
$= \left|\dfrac{\pi}{4} - \left(- \dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)\right|$
$= \left|\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right|= \dfrac{π}{2}

questions.q: The biquadratic equation, two of whose roots are $1+i, 1-\sqrt{2}$, is
questions.solution:
When $1+i, 1-i$ are the roots, then
Sum of the roots $=1+i+1-i=2$
and product of the roots $=1+1=2$
The equation is $x^2-2 x+2=0$
When $1-\sqrt{2}, 1+\sqrt{2}$ are the roots, then
Sum of the roots $=1-\sqrt{2}+1+\sqrt{2}=2$
Product of the roots $=1-2=-1$
The equation is $x^2-2 x-1=0$
The bi-quadratic equation is
$\$begin{array}{r}\left($x^2-2 x+2\right)\left(x²-2 x-1\right)=0 \\ \left(x⁴-(2+2) x³=(-1+4+2) x²\right. \\ =(2-4) x-2=0 \\ \Rightarrow \quad x⁴-4 x³+5 x²-2 x-2=0\end{array}

questions.q: $x^{3n} + y^{3n}$ is divisible by $x + y,$ if
questions.solution:
Let& $A = x^{3n} + y^{3n}$~

Put~$n = 0$, then

$A = x^{30} + y^{30} = x + y$

Hence, it is divisible by~$x + y$.

Let this be true for some natural number~$n = k$, then

$A = x^{3k} + y^{3k}$~is divisible by~$x + y$

$⇒ x^{3k} + y^{3k} = m ( x + y ) , m \in Z . . . ( 1 )$.

Now, for~$n = k + 1$,

$A = x^{3k + 1} + y^{3k + 1}$

$= x^{{3}^{k} \cdot 3} + y^{{3}^{k} \cdot 3}$

$= \left(x^{3k}\right)3 + \left(y^{3k}\right)3$

$= \left(x^{3k} + y^{3k}\right) \left[ \left($x^{3k}\right)2 + \left($y^{3k}\right)2 - x^{3k} \cdoty^{3k}\right]$~(using~$a^{3} + b^{3} = \left($a + b\right)\left(a^{2} - ab + b^{2}\right)$

$= m ( x + y ) \left[ \left($x^{3k}\right)2 + \left($y^{3k}\right)2 - x^{3k} \cdoty^{3k}\right]$~(using~$( 1 )$)

$⇒ x^{3k + 1} + y^{3k + 1}$~is divisible by~$x + y$~for all~$n ≥ 0, n \in Z$.

$

questions.q: If& $f  \left(x\right)$ is a polynomial of degree four with the leading coefficient one satisfying $f\left(1\right) = 1$, $f ( 2 ) = 2$~and~$f ( 3 ) = 3$,~then~\left[\dfrac{f  \left(- 1\right) + f \left(5\r$right)}{f\left($0\right) + $f\left($4\right)}\right]~(where~\left[\cdot\right]$represents the greatest integer function) is equal to$
questions.solution:
The roots of& $f \left($x\right) - x = 0$~are~$1$, $2$~and~$3$.

So, we get,

$f \left($x\right) - x = \left($x - 1\right)\left(x - 2\right) \left(x - 3\right)\left($x - a\right)$

For $x = - 1$, we get,

$f \left(-$1\right) + 1 = \left(-$2\right)\left(-$3\$right)\left(-4\right)\left(-$1 - a\right) = 24 \left($1 + a\right)$

For~$x = 5$, we get,

$f \left($5\right) - 5 = 4 $\cdot$3 $\cdot$2 \left(5 - a\right) = 24\left(5 - a\right)$

$f\left(- 1\right) + f\left(5\right) = \left(23 + 24a\right) + \left(125 - 24a\right) = 148$

For~$x = 0$, we get,

$f\left(0\right) - 0 = \left(- 1\right)\left(- 2\right)\left(- 3\right)\left(- a\right) = 6a$

For~$x = 4$, we get,

$f\left(4\right) - 4 = 3 \cdot 2 \cdot 1 \cdot \left(4 - a\right) = 24 - 6a$

$f\left(0\right) + f\left(4\right) = 28$

$\$left[\dfrac{f \left(-1\right) + f \left(5\right)}${f\left(0\right) + f\left(4\right)}\right] = \$left[\dfrac{148}{28}\right]

\left[\dfrac{f\left(- 1\right) + f\left(5\right)}{f\left(0\right) + f\left(4\right)}\right] =5$

$

questions.q: Let \(f(x)\) be a polynomial and \(a, b\) be distinct real numbers. Then the remainder in the division of \(f(x)\) by \((x-a)(x-b)\) is
questions.solution: Let \(f(x)=(x-a)(x-b) \cdot q(x)+r(x)\) Let \(r(x)=\alpha x+\beta \quad[\because \operatorname{deg} r(x) < \operatorname{deg}\). of divisor] \(\begin{aligned} \therefore \quad f(x) & =(x-a)(x-b) \cdot q(x)+\alpha x+\beta \\ f(a) & =\alpha a+\beta \quad \ldots (i) \\ f(b) & =\alpha b+\beta \quad \ldots (ii) \end{aligned}\) Subtract Eqs. (i) from (ii) \(\begin{aligned} f(a)-f(b) & =\alpha(a-b) \\ \alpha & $=\frac{f(a)-f(b)}{a-b}$\\ \alpha & $=\frac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a} \end{aligned}$\) Put, \(\alpha\) in Eq. (i) \(\begin{aligned} f(a) & $=\left(\frac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}\right) \times$a+\beta \\ f(a)[b-a] & =a f(b)-a f(a)+\beta(b-a) \\ b f(a)-a f(a) & =a f(b)-a f(a)+\beta(b-a) \\ \beta & $=\frac{b f(a)-a f(b)}{(b-a)}$\\ r(x) & =\alpha x+\beta \\ & $=\frac{f(b)-f(a) x}{b-a}+\frac{b f(a)-a f(b)}{(b-a)}$\\ & $=\frac{x f(b)-x f(a)+b f(a)-a f(b)}{b-a}$\\ r(x) & $=\frac{(x-a) f(b)+(b-x) f(a)}{b-a}$\\ r(x) & $=\frac{(x-a) f(b)-(x-b) f(a)}{b-a} \end{aligned}$\) Hence, option (c) is correct.

questions.q: The sum of all real values of $x$ satisfying the equation ${\left(x^{2} - 5x + 5\right)}^{x^{2} + 4x - 60} = 1$ is
questions.solution:
The given equation will be true in 3 cases.

Case 1: when $x^{2} - 5x + 5 = 1$

$⇒ x^{2} - 5x + 4 = 0$

$⇒ x = 1, 4$

Case 2: when $x^{2} + 4x - 60 = 0$

$⇒ x = 6, - 10$

Case 3: when $x^{2} - 5x + 5 = - 1$ and $x^{2} + 4x - 60 \in$ even integers

Now, $x^{2} - 5x + 5 = - 1$

$⇒ x = 2, 3$

Only $x = 2$ satisfies the given condition,

Hence, sum of all real values of $x$ is $1 + 4 + 6 - 10 + 2= 3$

questions.q: If $\alpha, \beta, \gamma$ are the roots of the equation $x^3-6 x^2+11 x-6=0$ and if $a=\alpha^2+\beta^2+\gamma^2$, $b=\alpha \beta+\beta \gamma+\gamma \alpha$ and $c=(\alpha+\beta)(\beta+\gamma)(\gamma+\alpha)$, then the correct inequality among the following is
questions.solution: Given equation $x^3-6 x^2+11 x-6=0$ has the roots $\alpha, \beta \gamma$. Given, $\quad a=\alpha^2+\beta^2+\gamma^2$ ...(i) $b=\alpha \beta+\beta \gamma+\gamma \alpha$ ...(ii) $c=(\alpha+\beta)(\beta+\gamma)(\gamma+\alpha)$ ...(iii) In cubic equation the sum of the roots $\alpha+\beta+\gamma=-\left(\frac{-6}{1}\right)=6\alpha \beta+\beta \gamma+\gamma \alpha=\left(\frac{11}{1}\right)=11$ product of the roots $\alpha \cdot \beta \cdot \gamma=-\left(\frac{-6}{1}\right)=6$ From Eq. (ii), $b=11$ From Eq. (i), $a=\alpha^2+\beta^2+\gamma^2\Rightarrow \quad a=(\alpha+\beta+\gamma)^2-2(\alpha \beta+\beta \gamma+\gamma \alpha)\Rightarrow \quad a=(6)^2-2(11) \Rightarrow 36-22\Rightarrow \quad a=14$ From Eq. (iii) $c=(\alpha+\beta)(\beta+\gamma)(\gamma+\alpha)=\left(\alpha \beta+\beta^2+\alpha \gamma+\beta \gamma\right)(\gamma+\alpha)=\alpha \beta \gamma+\beta^2 \gamma+\alpha \gamma^2+\beta \gamma^2+\alpha^2 \beta+\alpha \beta^2+\alpha^2 \gamma+\alpha \beta \gamma\Rightarrow c=[(\alpha+\beta+\gamma)-\gamma][(\alpha+\beta+\gamma)-\alpha][(\alpha+\beta+\gamma)-\beta]=(6-\gamma)(6-\alpha)(6-\beta)=(36-6 \gamma-6 \alpha+\alpha \gamma)(6-\beta)=216-36 \gamma-36 \alpha+6 \alpha \gamma-36 \beta+6 \gamma \beta+6 \alpha \beta-\alpha \beta \gamma=216-\alpha \beta \gamma+6(\alpha \beta+\beta \gamma+\gamma \alpha)-36(\alpha+\beta+\gamma)=216-6+6(11)-36(6)=210+66-216=60$ Hence, $\quad c=60\Rightarrow \quad b < a < c$Alternate method Given equation is $x^3-6 x^2+11 x-6=0\Rightarrow \quad(x-1)(x-2)(x-3)=0$ The roots of this equation are 1,2 , and 3 . Let $\alpha=1, \beta=2, \gamma=3$ Now, $\quad a=\alpha^2+\beta^2+\gamma^2=1+4+9=14b=\alpha \beta+\beta \gamma+\gamma \alpha=2+6+3=11c=(\alpha+\beta)(\beta+\gamma)(\gamma+\alpha)=3 \cdot 5 \cdot 4=60$ From the values of $a, b$ and $c$ it is clear that $b < a < c$.

questions.q: If $\alpha, \beta$ are the roots of $x^2+p x+q=0$, then the values of $\alpha^3+\beta^3$ and $\alpha^4+\alpha^2 \beta^2+\beta^4$ are respectively ...... and ......
options: \left(3 p q-p^3\right)$ and  \left(p^4-3 p^2 q+3 q^2\right)$
questions.solution: Since $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are roots of equation $\begin{aligned}$& x^2+p x+q=0, \text { so } \\ & \alpha+\beta=-p \text { and } \alpha \beta=q \end{aligned} As we know that, $\alpha^3+\beta^3=(\alpha+\beta) \left(\alpha^2+\beta^2-\alpha \beta\right)\begin{aligned}$& =(\alpha+\beta)\left[(\alpha+\beta)^2-3 \alpha \beta\right] \\ & =(-p)\left[p^2-3 q\right]=3 p q-p^3 \\ \text { and } & \alpha^4+\alpha^2 \beta^2+\beta^4 \\ & =\left(\alpha^2+\beta^2\right)^2-\alpha^2 \beta^2=\left[(\alpha+\beta)^2-2 \alpha \beta\right]^2-(\alpha \beta)^2 \\ & =\left((-p)^2-2 q\right)^2-q^2 \\ & =\left(p^2-2 q\right)^2-q^2=\left(p^2-2 q-q\right)\left(p^2-2 q+q\right) \\ & =\left(p^2-q\right)\left(p^2-3 q\right) \end{aligned}

questions.q:
If $m_1$ and $m_2$ are the roots of the equation
$x^2+(\sqrt{3}+2) x+(\sqrt{3}-1)=0,$
then the area of the triangle formed by the lines $y=m_1 x, y=m_2 x$ and $y=c$
questions.solution:
Since, $m_1$ and $m_2$ are the roots of the equation $x^2+(\sqrt{3}+2) x+(\sqrt{3}-1)=0$
then $\quad m_1+m_2=-(\sqrt{3}+2)$,
$m_1 m_2=\sqrt{3}-1\therefore m_1-m_2=\sqrt{\left(m_1+m_2\right)^2-4 m_1 m_2}=\sqrt{(3+4+4 \sqrt{3}-4 \sqrt{3}+4)}=\sqrt{11}$
and coordinates of the vertices of the given triangles are $(0,0),  \left(c / m_1, c\right)$ and  \left(c / m_2, c\right)$. Hence, the required area of triangle
=\frac{1}{2}\left|\begin{array}{ccc}$0 & 0 & 1 \\ $\frac{c}{m_1}$& c & 1 \\ $\frac{c}{m_2}$& c & 1\end{array}\right|$=\frac{1}{2}$c^2\left|\left(\frac{1}{m_1}-\frac{1}{m_2}\right)\right|=\frac{1}{2}c^2 \frac{\left|m_2-m_1\right|}{m_1 m_2}=\frac{1}{2}c^2 \frac{\sqrt{11}}{(\sqrt{3}-1)}=\frac{1}{2}c^2 \cdot \frac{\sqrt{11} \cdot(\sqrt{3}+1)}{(\sqrt{3}-1)(\sqrt{3}+1)}=\left(\frac{\sqrt{33}+\sqrt{11}}{4}\right) \cdotc^2

questions.q: The equation $x^3+x-1=0$ has
questions.solution: Let $\mathrm{f}(x)=x^3+x-1$ A root of $\mathrm{f}(x)$ exists, if $\mathrm{f}(x)=0$ for at least one value of $x$. $\begin{aligned}$& $\mathrm{f}($0)=-1 < 0 \\ & \mathrm{f}(1)=1>0 \end{aligned} $\therefore \quad$ By intermediate value theorem, there has to be a point ' $c$ ' between 0 and 1 such that $\mathrm{f}(x)=0$. $\therefore \quad$ The given equation has exactly one real root. Alternate Method: Let $\mathrm{f}(x)=x^3+x-1\begin{array}{ll} \therefore \quad \mathrmf^{\prime}($x)=3 x²+1 \\ \quad \Rightarrow \mathrmf^{\prime}(x)>0 \quad \forall x \in $\mathrm{R} \end{array}\Rightarrow \mathrm{f}(x)$ is an increasing function. $\Rightarrow \mathrm{f}(x)$ intersects $\mathrm{X}$-axis at only one point. $\therefore \quad$ The given equation has exactly one real root.

questions.q: If the bi-quadratic equation $f ( x ) = x^{4} + 2x^{3} - 16x^{2} - 22x + 7 = 0$~has $2 + \sqrt{3}$ as one of its roots, then which of the following is not a root of $f\left(x\right) ?$
questions.solution:
Given,& $f ( x ) = x^{4} + 2x^{3} - 16x^{2} - 22x + 7 = 0$

$∵ 2 + \sqrt{3}$~is one of the roots of~$f\left(x\right) = 0$

$∴ 2 - \sqrt{3}$~is also one of the roots of~$f\left(x\right) = 0$

Let us assume the other two roots of the~$f\left(x\right) = 0$~are~$\alpha, \beta$

$⇒$~Sum of roots$= - 2$

$⇒ \alpha + \beta + 2 + \sqrt{3} + 2 - \sqrt{3} = - 2$

$⇒ \alpha + \beta = - 6 \ldots \left(i\right)$

And product of roots$= 7$

$⇒ \alpha\beta \left($2 + $\sqrt{3}\right)\left($2 - $\sqrt{3}\right) =$7$

$⇒ $\alpha\beta =$7 \ldots \left($ii\right)$

Put~\beta = \dfrac{7}{α}~in equation~ \left(i\right)$, we get

$⇒ {α}^{2} + 6\alpha +7 = 0$

$⇒ \alpha = $\dfrac{- 6 \pm \sqrt{36 - 28}}{2} = -$3 \pm $\sqrt{2}

Put value of~$\alpha$~in equation~ \left(ii\right)$, we get

$\beta = -3 ∓ $\sqrt{2}

$∴$~Roots of the~$f\left(x\right) = 0$~are~$2 + $\sqrt{3},$2 - $\sqrt{3}, -$3 + $\sqrt{2}, -$3 - \sqrt{2}.$

questions.q: Let $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are the roots of equation $ax^{2} + bx + c = 0\left(a \ne 0\right) .$ If $1, \alpha + \beta, \alpha\beta$ are in arithmetic progression and $\alpha, 2, \beta$ are in harmonic progression, then the value of $\dfrac{{\alpha}^{2} + {\beta}^{2} - 2{\alpha}^{2}{\beta}^{2}}{2\left({\alpha}^{2} + {\beta}^{2}\right)}$ is equal to
questions.solution:
$1,\alpha + \beta, \alpha\beta$ are in A.P. $⇒ 1, \dfrac{- b}{a}, \dfrac{c}{a}$ are in A.P.
$⇒ 1 + \dfrac{c}{a} = \dfrac{- 2b}{a} ⇒ a + c + 2b = 0$ … \left(1\right)$
$\dfrac{1}{\alpha}, \dfrac{1}{2}, \dfrac{1}{\beta}$ are in A.P. $⇒ \dfrac{1}{\alpha} + \dfrac{1}{\beta} = 1 ⇒ \alpha + \beta = \alpha\beta$
$⇒ \dfrac{- b}{a} = \dfrac{c}{a} ⇒ b + c = 0$ … \left(2\right)$
From \left(1\right)$ & \left(2\right)$ we get,
$a = - b = c$
$⇒ \alpha, \beta$ are roots of equation $x^{2} - x + 1 = 0$
Now, $\dfrac{{\alpha}^{2} + {\beta}^{2} - 2{\alpha}^{2}{\beta}^{2}}{2\left({\alpha}^{2} + {\beta}^{2}\right)} = \dfrac{1}{2} - \dfrac{( \alpha\beta{)}^{2}}{( \alpha + \beta{)}^{2} - 2\alpha\beta}$
$= \dfrac{1}{2} - \dfrac{{\left(1\right)}^{2}}{{\left(1\right)}^{2} - 2\left(1\right)} = \dfrac{1}{2} + 1 = 1.5$

questions.q: The sum of the roots of the equation,$x^{2} + | 2x - 3 | - 4 = 0$ , is
questions.solution:
Given Equation :$x^{2} + | 2x - 3 | - 4 = 0$

$\text{x} < \dfrac{3}{2} ⇒ x^{2} - \left(\text{2x} - 3\right) - 4 = 0$

⇒$x^{2} - 2x - 1 = 0$

Roots $\alpha \text{,} \beta = \dfrac{2 \pm \sqrt{4 + 4}}{2} = 1 \pm \sqrt{2}$

root $1 + \sqrt{2} > \dfrac{3}{2}$, hence rejected

⇒ root accepted $1 - \sqrt{2}$

$\text{x} \ge \dfrac{3}{2} ⇒ x^{2} + \left(\text{2x} - 3\right) - 4 = 0$

⇒ x2 + 2x - 7 = 0

Roots $\gamma \text{,} \delta = \dfrac{- 2 \pm \sqrt{4 + 4 \times 7}}{2} - 1 \pm 2 \sqrt{2}$

root $- 1 - 2 \sqrt{2} < \dfrac{3}{2}$, hence rejected

⇒ root accepted $- 1 + 2 \sqrt{2}$

Sum of roots $= \left(1 - \sqrt{2}\right) + \left(- 1 + 2 \sqrt{2}\right) = \sqrt{2}$

questions.q: Let $p$ and $q$ be roots of the equation $x^{2} - 2x + A = 0$~and let $r$ and $s$ be the roots of the equation $x^{2} - 18x + B = 0 .$~If $p < q < r < s$ are in $AP,$ then $A$ and $B$& are
questions.solution:
Let the four numbers in $A . P .$~be

$p = a - 3d, q = a - d, r = a + d, s = a + 3d$.

Now,~$p$~and~$q$~are the roots of the quadratic equation~$x^{2} - 2x + A = 0$.

Therefore, using the sum~and product of roots of a quadratic equation, we get

$p + q = 2 \ldots \left(i\right)$

$pq = A \ldots \left(ii\right)$

And,~$r, s$~are the roots of the quadratic equation~$x^{2} - 18x + B = 0$.

Therefore,

$r + s = 18 \ldots \left(iii\right)$

$rs = B \ldots \left($iv\right)$

By~ \left($i\right)$~and~ \left($iii\right)$, we have

$p + q + r + s = 4a = 20$

$⇒ a = 5$

Now,

$p + q = 2$

$⇒ 10 - 4d = 2$

$⇒ d = 2 .$

Also,~

$r + s = 18$

$⇒ 10 + 4d = 18$

$⇒ d = 2 .$

Hence, the numbers are~$- 1, 3, 7, 11 .$

Therefore,~$pq = A = - 3, rs = B = 77 .$

$
